nodes.label: What's new — weekly Claude Code dev digest
nodes.rationale: A weekly digest of notable Claude Code features with code snippets, demos, and context on why they matter. It covers only the features most likely to change how you work; every bug fix and minor improvement lives in the changelog instead. As captured, it runs from Week 13 (March 2026) to Week 29 (July 2026).

nodes.label: Digest vs changelog — a deliberate split
nodes.rationale: The digest carries only notable, workflow-changing features with runnable code and a demo; the changelog carries every bug fix and minor improvement. Looking for a specific fix means reading the changelog, not this page.

nodes.label: Week 29 (July 13-17, 2026) — v2.1.207-v2.1.212
nodes.rationale: Headline: artifacts call your MCP connectors — a published artifact pulls live data and takes actions through each VIEWER's own MCP connectors when they open the page. Also public sharing links, editor roles on Team and Enterprise, and artifacts created from Claude Tag sessions.

nodes.label: Artifacts call the viewer's own MCP connectors
nodes.rationale: A published artifact can pull live data and take actions through each viewer's own MCP connectors when they open the page — so the page's data access follows the reader, not the author. Shipped Week 29.

nodes.label: Screen reader mode
nodes.rationale: Replaces the visual terminal interface with plain, linear text for screen readers such as VoiceOver and NVDA. Shipped Week 29.

nodes.label: /fork copies the conversation into a background session
nodes.rationale: `/fork` copies your conversation into a new background session while you keep working in the original. Shipped Week 29.

nodes.label: Week 28 (July 6-10, 2026) — v2.1.202-v2.1.206
nodes.rationale: Headline: an in-app browser on Desktop, so Claude can pull up docs, designs or any site and interact with pages the way it does with a local dev-server preview. Also `/doctor` (alias `/checkup`), auto mode blocking transcript tampering, and agent-view rows with a colored state word and classifier-written headline.

nodes.label: /doctor — full setup checkup that can fix issues
nodes.rationale: `/doctor` diagnoses setup issues and can fix them, with `/checkup` as its alias. Shipped Week 28.

nodes.label: Week 27 (June 29 - July 3, 2026) — v2.1.195-v2.1.201
nodes.rationale: Headline: Claude Sonnet 5 becomes the default for Pro, Team Standard and Enterprise subscription seats — top-tier coding and tool use at Sonnet pricing, a native 1M-token context window, and adaptive thinking on by default. Also Claude in Chrome GA, background-by-default subagents, Claude Desktop on Linux beta, and `/radio`.

nodes.label: Claude Sonnet 5 — native 1M context at Sonnet pricing
nodes.rationale: The new default model for Pro, Team Standard and Enterprise subscription seats: top-tier coding and tool use at Sonnet pricing, a native 1M-token context window, and adaptive thinking on by default. Shipped Week 27.

nodes.label: Subagents run in the background by default
nodes.rationale: Subagents became background-by-default so Claude keeps working while they run, rather than blocking the main turn. Shipped Week 27.

nodes.label: Week 26 (June 22-26, 2026) — v2.1.185-v2.1.193
nodes.rationale: Headline: `claude mcp login` authenticates a configured MCP server from the shell instead of the interactive `/mcp` menu, with `claude mcp logout` to clear stored credentials. Also shell mode responding to command output, `/rewind` resuming from before a `/clear`, and background subagents surfacing permission prompts in the main session instead of auto-denying.

nodes.label: claude mcp login / logout from the shell
nodes.rationale: Authenticate a configured MCP server from your shell rather than the interactive `/mcp` menu, and clear its stored credentials later with `claude mcp logout`. Shipped Week 26.

nodes.label: Background subagents surface permission prompts instead of auto-denying
nodes.rationale: Background subagents now raise permission prompts in the main session rather than auto-denying them — a behavior change that makes a background subagent's blocked action visible rather than silent. Shipped Week 26.

nodes.label: Week 25 (June 15-19, 2026) — v2.1.178-v2.1.183
nodes.rationale: Headline: Artifacts — turn a session's output into a live, shareable page on claude.ai that updates in place as the session works, in beta on Team and Enterprise. Also parameter-matching deny/ask rules, `/config key=value`, and auto mode blocking destructive git commands.

nodes.label: Deny and ask rules match tool parameters
nodes.rationale: Permission rules gained parameter matching with the `Tool(param:value)` form, for example `Agent(model:opus)` — so a rule can target a specific argument rather than the whole tool. Shipped Week 25.

nodes.label: Week 24 (June 8-12, 2026) — v2.1.166-v2.1.176
nodes.rationale: Headline: `/cd` moves the current session to a new working directory mid-conversation WITHOUT rebuilding the prompt cache. Also nested sub-agents (background chains capped at five levels deep), `--safe-mode`, and `fallbackModel` configuring up to three fallbacks tried in order.

nodes.label: Sub-agents can spawn sub-agents, capped at five levels
nodes.rationale: Sub-agents gained the ability to spawn their own sub-agents, with background chains capped at five levels deep. Shipped Week 24.

nodes.label: --safe-mode disables all customizations
nodes.rationale: `--safe-mode` starts Claude Code with all customizations disabled for troubleshooting — the standard control arm when a session misbehaves and you need to know whether your own config is the cause. Shipped Week 24.

nodes.label: Week 23 (June 1-5, 2026) — v2.1.158-v2.1.165
nodes.rationale: Headline: auto mode reaches Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform and Microsoft Foundry for Opus 4.7 and Opus 4.8, replacing permission prompts with background safety checks. Also safer automatic edits, `/plugin list`, and version requirements for managed deployments.

nodes.label: Version requirements for managed deployments
nodes.rationale: Managed deployments can require an approved Claude Code version range — the fleet-level counterpart to the per-feature version floors elsewhere in the docs. Shipped Week 23.

nodes.label: Week 22 (May 25-29, 2026) — v2.1.150-v2.1.157
nodes.rationale: Headline: Claude Opus 4.8 becomes the default for Max, Team Premium, Enterprise pay-as-you-go and Anthropic API accounts, with high effort by default and `/effort xhigh` for the hardest tasks. Also dynamic workflows, the security-guidance plugin, and fast mode on Opus 4.8 at $10/$50 per MTok.

nodes.label: Dynamic workflows orchestrate dozens to hundreds of subagents
nodes.rationale: Dynamic workflows orchestrate dozens to hundreds of subagents from a script Claude writes — the mechanism behind the `ultracode` setting and the parallelism guidance elsewhere. Shipped Week 22.

nodes.label: security-guidance plugin reviews Claude's own changes
nodes.rationale: The security-guidance plugin reviews Claude's changes for vulnerabilities as it works, rather than only at review time. Shipped Week 22.

nodes.label: Week 21 (May 18-22, 2026) — v2.1.143-v2.1.149
nodes.rationale: Headline: auto mode reaches the Pro plan and supports Sonnet 4.6 alongside Opus. Also `/usage` breaking limits down by skill, subagent, plugin and MCP server; the new `/code-review` command reporting correctness bugs; and background sessions appearing in `/resume` and staying alive when pinned.

nodes.label: /usage attributes plan limits by component
nodes.rationale: `/usage` breaks down what drives your plan limits by skill, subagent, plugin and MCP server — attribution rather than a single total. Shipped Week 21 (and shown again in Week 16).

nodes.label: Week 20 (May 11-15, 2026) — v2.1.139-v2.1.142
nodes.rationale: Headline: agent view — `claude agents` opens one screen for every Claude Code session, showing what's running, what's blocked on you, and what's done. Also `/goal`, fast mode on Opus 4.7 by default, and 'Summarize up to here' in the Rewind menu.

nodes.label: /goal keeps Claude working until a completion condition holds
nodes.rationale: `/goal` keeps Claude working across turns until a completion condition holds — the feature that makes an unattended multi-turn round possible, and the reason the condition's wording matters. Shipped Week 20.

nodes.label: Week 19 (May 4-8, 2026) — v2.1.128-v2.1.136
nodes.rationale: Headline: plugins load from `.zip` archives and URLs — `--plugin-dir` accepts `.zip` files and `--plugin-url` fetches a plugin archive for the session. Also `worktree.baseRef`, auto mode hard deny rules that block unconditionally regardless of allow exceptions, and hooks seeing the active effort level.

nodes.label: Auto mode hard deny rules block unconditionally
nodes.rationale: Hard deny rules block actions unconditionally regardless of allow exceptions — an allow rule cannot re-open what a hard deny closes. Shipped Week 19.

nodes.label: Hooks see the active effort level
nodes.rationale: Hooks gained access to the active effort level via `effort.level` and the `$CLAUDE_EFFORT` environment variable, so a hook can branch on how hard the session is thinking. Shipped Week 19.

nodes.label: Week 18 (April 27 - May 1, 2026) — v2.1.120-v2.1.126
nodes.rationale: Headline: Windows no longer requires Git for Windows — Claude Code uses PowerShell as the shell tool when Bash is absent. Also `claude ultrareview` bringing cloud code review to CI and scripts, `claude project purge`, and pasting a PR URL into `/resume` to find the session that created it.

nodes.label: claude ultrareview brings cloud review to CI and scripts
nodes.rationale: `claude ultrareview` exposes cloud code review to CI and scripts, rather than only the interactive `/ultrareview` slash command. Shipped Week 18.

nodes.label: Week 17 (April 20-24, 2026) — v2.1.114-v2.1.119
nodes.rationale: Headline: `/ultrareview` opens as a public research preview — a fleet of bug-hunting agents runs in the cloud and findings land back in the CLI or Desktop automatically. Also session recap for unfocused terminals, custom themes shippable from `/theme` or a plugin, and a redesigned Claude Code on the web.

nodes.label: Week 16 (April 13-17, 2026) — v2.1.105-v2.1.113
nodes.rationale: Headline: Claude Opus 4.7 becomes the default on Max and Team Premium, introducing the `xhigh` effort level as the recommended setting for most coding work plus an interactive `/effort` slider. Also Routines on the web, mobile push notifications, `/usage`, and the CLI moving to native binaries.

nodes.label: Routines fire templated cloud agents on a trigger
nodes.rationale: Routines on Claude Code on the web fire templated cloud agents from a schedule, a GitHub event, or an API call. Shipped Week 16.

nodes.label: The CLI moved to native binaries
nodes.rationale: Claude Code's CLI moved to native binaries in Week 16 — a distribution change underlying the later Windows/PowerShell and install-troubleshooting material.

nodes.label: Week 15 (April 6-10, 2026) — v2.1.92-v2.1.101
nodes.rationale: Headline: Ultraplan enters early preview — draft a plan in the cloud from the CLI, review and comment on it in a web editor, then run it remotely or pull it back local, with the first run auto-creating a cloud environment. Also the Monitor tool, `/loop` self-pacing when the interval is omitted, `/team-onboarding`, and `/autofix-pr`.

nodes.label: The Monitor tool streams background events into the conversation
nodes.rationale: Monitor streams background events into the conversation so Claude can tail logs and react live, rather than polling. Shipped Week 15.

nodes.label: /loop self-paces when the interval is omitted
nodes.rationale: `/loop` gained a dynamic mode: omit the interval and the model decides when to wake itself up rather than running on a fixed cadence. Shipped Week 15.

nodes.label: Week 14 (March 30 - April 3, 2026) — v2.1.86-v2.1.91
nodes.rationale: Headline: computer use comes to the CLI in research preview — Claude opens native apps, clicks through UI and verifies changes from the terminal, best for closing the loop on things only a GUI can verify. Also `/powerup` lessons, flicker-free alt-screen rendering, a per-tool MCP result-size override up to 500K, and plugin executables on the Bash tool's PATH.

nodes.label: Computer use in the CLI — for what only a GUI can verify
nodes.rationale: Computer use lets Claude open native apps, click through UI and verify changes from the terminal. The docs scope it explicitly: it is best for closing the loop on things only a GUI can verify, not as a general automation surface. Shipped Week 14.

nodes.label: Week 13 (March 23-27, 2026) — v2.1.83-v2.1.85
nodes.rationale: The earliest week captured. Headline: auto mode lands in research preview — a classifier handles permission prompts so safe actions run uninterrupted and risky ones get blocked, positioned as the middle ground between approving everything and `--dangerously-skip-permissions`. Also computer use in Desktop, PR auto-fix on Web, `/` transcript search, a native PowerShell tool, and conditional `if` hooks.

nodes.label: Auto mode — the middle ground on permissions
nodes.rationale: A classifier handles permission prompts so safe actions run without interruption and risky ones are blocked — explicitly positioned as the middle ground between approving everything and `--dangerously-skip-permissions`. Introduced Week 13 and extended in Weeks 19, 21, 23, 25 and 28.

nodes.label: Auto mode hardened across five later weeks
nodes.rationale: Reading the digest end to end, auto mode is the single most-iterated feature: research preview (W13), hard deny rules (W19), Pro plan and Sonnet 4.6 (W21), third-party providers (W23), blocking destructive git commands (W25), and blocking transcript tampering plus asking before `rm -rf` on unresolved variables (W28).

nodes.label: Keep Claude working toward a goal (/goal)
nodes.rationale: `/goal` sets a completion condition and Claude keeps working across turns until it is met. After each turn a small fast model checks whether the condition holds; if not, Claude starts another turn instead of returning control. The goal clears automatically once the condition is met. Requires Claude Code v2.1.139 or later.

nodes.label: Use a goal for substantial work with a verifiable end state
nodes.rationale: The documented fits: migrating a module until every call site compiles and tests pass, implementing a design doc until all acceptance criteria hold, splitting a large file until each part is under a size budget, and working a labeled issue backlog until the queue is empty. The common shape is a VERIFIABLE end state, not merely a long task.

nodes.label: Three ways to keep a session running, chosen by what starts the next turn
nodes.rationale: `/goal` starts the next turn when the previous one finishes and stops when a model confirms the condition; `/loop` starts on a time interval and stops when you stop it or Claude decides the work is done; a Stop hook starts after the previous turn and stops when your own script or prompt decides.

nodes.label: /goal is session-scoped; a Stop hook is settings-scoped
nodes.rationale: Both fire after every turn. `/goal` is a shortcut you type, active for the current session only. A Stop hook lives in a settings file, applies to every session in its scope, and can run a SCRIPT for deterministic checks or a PROMPT for model-evaluated ones — which is the reason to write one instead of using `/goal`.

nodes.label: /goal and auto mode remove different prompts
nodes.rationale: Auto mode approves tool calls WITHIN a turn but never starts a new one — Claude still stops when it judges the work done. `/goal` adds a separate evaluator that checks the condition AFTER every turn. They are complementary: auto mode removes per-tool prompts, `/goal` removes per-turn prompts.

nodes.label: Completion is decided by a fresh model, not the one doing the work
nodes.rationale: The stated reason `/goal` differs from Claude simply stopping when it thinks it is finished: a separate evaluator judges the condition, so 'done' is not self-assessed by the model that did the work.

nodes.label: One goal per session; the same command sets, checks and clears
nodes.rationale: Only one goal can be active per session, and a new one REPLACES the active one. `/goal <condition>` sets, `/goal` with no argument shows status, `/goal clear` removes.

nodes.label: Setting a goal starts a turn immediately
nodes.rationale: The condition itself becomes the directive for that first turn — no separate prompt is needed. While the goal is active a `◎ /goal active` indicator shows how long it has been running.

nodes.label: A goal does not change permissions
nodes.rationale: In the default permission mode Claude still asks before tool calls the settings do not already allow — including the very test command a condition names. To let goal turns run unattended, pair `/goal` with auto mode. A goal alone does not make a round unattended.

nodes.label: The evaluator judges the conversation, not the filesystem
nodes.rationale: The evaluator does NOT run commands or read files independently, so the condition must be something Claude's own output can demonstrate. 'All tests in test/auth pass' works because Claude runs the tests and the result lands in the transcript for the evaluator to read. This is the single constraint that decides whether a condition is writable.

nodes.label: A durable condition has three parts
nodes.rationale: One measurable end state (a test result, a build exit code, a file count, an empty queue); a stated check saying how Claude should prove it (`npm test` exits 0, `git status` is clean); and constraints that matter — anything that must NOT change on the way there, such as 'no other test file is modified'.

nodes.label: The condition can be up to 4,000 characters
nodes.rationale: A hard limit on the condition text itself, which is what makes an unbounded rider document a separate artifact from the goal payload.

nodes.label: Bound a goal with a turn or time clause inside the condition
nodes.rationale: There is no separate turn-limit flag: to bound how long a goal runs, include a clause such as `or stop after 20 turns` IN the condition. Claude reports progress against that clause each turn and the evaluator judges it from the conversation — so the bound is model-evaluated, not enforced by the runtime.

nodes.label: /goal status fields
nodes.rationale: An active goal reports the condition, how long it has run, how many turns have been evaluated, the current token spend, and the evaluator's most recent reason. The turn count and reason appear only after the first evaluation has run. If no goal is active but one was achieved earlier, the status shows the achieved condition with its duration, turns and spend.

nodes.label: The evaluator's reason becomes guidance for the next turn
nodes.rationale: On a 'no' the evaluator returns a short reason and Claude takes it as guidance for the next turn; the most recent reason appears in the status view and the transcript. The evaluator is therefore a steering signal, not only a stop signal.

nodes.label: /goal clear and its aliases
nodes.rationale: `/goal clear` removes an active goal, printing `Goal cleared:` and the condition, or `No goal set`. `stop`, `off`, `reset`, `none` and `cancel` are accepted aliases. Running `/clear` to start a new conversation also removes any active goal.

nodes.label: Resume restores the condition but resets the counters
nodes.rationale: A goal still active when a session ended is restored on `--resume`/`--continue`, but the turn count, timer, and token-spend baseline ALL reset. A goal already achieved or cleared is not restored. So a turn-bound clause silently gets a fresh budget after a resume.

nodes.label: /goal in non-interactive mode runs the loop to completion
nodes.rationale: `claude -p "/goal <condition>"` runs the whole loop in one invocation. It also works in the desktop app and through Remote Control. With default text output NOTHING prints until the condition is met, so a long goal looks stuck — add `--output-format stream-json --verbose` to emit each message. Ctrl+C interrupts.

nodes.label: /goal is a wrapper around a session-scoped prompt-based Stop hook
nodes.rationale: Each time Claude finishes a turn, Claude Code sends the condition and the conversation so far to the configured small fast model, which answers yes or no with a short reason. This implementation detail is what makes the hooks-system requirements below apply.

nodes.label: The evaluator runs on the small fast model
nodes.rationale: It defaults to Haiku on the Claude API; on a third-party provider the platform's default applies. It runs on whichever provider the session is configured for, does not call tools, and its tokens are billed on that model — typically negligible against main-turn spend.

nodes.label: ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL is not /goal-specific
nodes.rationale: Setting it to change the evaluator's model ALSO resolves the `haiku` alias to that model and runs all background functionality — such as conversation summarization — on it. Claude Code reads it everywhere it uses the small fast model, so this is a global change wearing a local disguise.

nodes.label: /goal requires trust and unrestricted hooks
nodes.rationale: Because the evaluator is part of the hooks system, `/goal` runs only in workspaces where the trust dialog has been accepted, and is unavailable when `disableAllHooks` is set at ANY settings level or `allowManagedHooksOnly` is set in managed settings. In each case the command says why rather than silently doing nothing.

nodes.label: /goal requires v2.1.139 or later
nodes.rationale: A hard version floor stated at the top of the page. On an older Claude Code the command does not exist, which is a different failure from the trust/hooks unavailability described under Requirements.

nodes.label: /goal row — finishes a turn, stops on a model's confirmation
nodes.rationale: In the comparison table: the next turn starts when the previous turn FINISHES, and the loop stops when a model confirms the condition is met. Turn-driven, not clock-driven.

nodes.label: /loop row — time-interval driven
nodes.rationale: The next turn starts when a TIME INTERVAL elapses, and it stops when you stop it or Claude decides the work is done. No condition is evaluated, so nothing external judges completion.

nodes.label: Stop hook row — turn-driven with your own stop rule
nodes.rationale: The next turn starts when the previous one finishes, and it stops when your own script or prompt decides. Same trigger as `/goal`, different decider.

nodes.label: Scheduling runs work independent of any open session
nodes.rationale: A tip distinguishing the three continuation approaches, which all keep the CURRENT session running, from cloud routines and desktop scheduled tasks — nightly tests, morning triage — which need no open session at all.

nodes.label: The documented example condition
nodes.rationale: `/goal all tests in test/auth pass and the lint step is clean` — one measurable end state plus a named check, in the form the evaluator can read out of the transcript.

nodes.label: The ◎ /goal active indicator
nodes.rationale: While a goal is active, an indicator shows how long it has been running — the only always-visible sign a session is in a goal loop rather than waiting for you.

nodes.label: Setting a goal while one is active REPLACES it
nodes.rationale: There is no stack and no confirmation: the new condition silently takes over from the old one. Combined with one-goal-per-session, this means a mistyped `/goal` discards the running condition.

nodes.label: Non-interactive text output prints NOTHING until the condition is met
nodes.rationale: With the default text output format a `-p` goal that runs many turns looks stuck, because no message is emitted until completion. `--output-format stream-json --verbose` emits each message as the loop runs; Ctrl+C interrupts.

nodes.label: Evaluation tokens are billed on the small fast model and are typically negligible
nodes.rationale: Billed against the small fast model configured for your provider, and the docs characterize the spend as negligible compared to main-turn spend — so the evaluator is not a meaningful part of a goal's cost.

nodes.label: The evaluator does not call tools
nodes.rationale: Stated separately from the transcript-only constraint: it cannot invoke anything, so it can never independently confirm a claim Claude made. Every check must already be visible in the conversation.

nodes.label: The goal clears itself once the condition is met
nodes.rationale: On a 'yes' Claude Code clears the goal and records an ACHIEVED entry in the transcript, which is what the status view later reports with duration, turn count and token spend.

nodes.label: Push events into a running session with channels
nodes.rationale: A channel is an MCP server that PUSHES events into your already-running Claude Code session, so Claude can react to things that happen while you are not at the terminal — CI results, chat messages, monitoring events. Channels can be two-way: Claude reads the event and replies back through the same channel.

nodes.label: Channels are a research preview
nodes.rationale: Availability is rolling out gradually and both the `--channels` flag syntax and the protocol contract may change. Neither `--channels` nor `--dangerously-load-development-channels` appears in `claude --help` while in preview — the flags work even though they are not listed, so their absence from help is not evidence they do not exist.

nodes.label: Channels require Anthropic authentication
nodes.rationale: They require authentication through claude.ai or a Console API key and are NOT available on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, or Microsoft Foundry. Team and Enterprise organizations must explicitly enable them.

nodes.label: Events arrive only while the session is open
nodes.rationale: A channel delivers into a live session, so an always-on setup means running Claude in a background process or persistent terminal. There is no store-and-forward for a closed session.

nodes.label: You see the inbound message but not the reply text
nodes.rationale: When Claude replies through a channel the terminal shows the tool call and a confirmation such as 'sent'; the actual reply text appears only on the other platform. So the terminal is not a full transcript of a channel conversation.

nodes.label: Telegram, Discord and iMessage ship in the preview
nodes.rationale: Each supported channel is a plugin from `claude-plugins-official` and each requires Bun, because the pre-built channel plugins are Bun scripts. You install a channel as a plugin and configure it with your own credentials.

nodes.label: Telegram channel setup
nodes.rationale: Create a bot with BotFather (`/newbot`, username ending in `bot`), install `telegram@claude-plugins-official` at USER scope, run `/telegram:configure <token>` (saved to `~/.claude/channels/telegram/.env`, or set `TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN`), restart with `--channels`, then pair with `/telegram:access pair <code>` and lock down with `/telegram:access policy allowlist`.

nodes.label: Discord channel setup
nodes.rationale: Create an application in the Developer Portal, reset and copy the bot token, ENABLE Message Content Intent under Privileged Gateway Intents, invite the bot with the `bot` scope plus View Channels / Send Messages / Send Messages in Threads / Read Message History / Attach Files / Add Reactions, then install, `/discord:configure <token>`, restart with `--channels`, pair and set the allowlist policy.

nodes.label: iMessage channel setup — no bot, no token
nodes.rationale: It reads the Messages database at `~/Library/Messages/chat.db` directly and sends replies through AppleScript, so it requires macOS and needs no bot token or external service. Full Disk Access must be granted to whichever app launched Bun, or the server exits immediately with `authorization denied`. The first reply triggers a macOS Automation prompt.

nodes.label: iMessage self-chat bypasses access control
nodes.rationale: Texting yourself reaches Claude immediately with no setup — by default only your own messages pass through. Other contacts are added by handle with `/imessage:access allow +15551234567`, where a handle is a `+country` phone number or an Apple ID email.

nodes.label: fakechat — the zero-credential demo channel
nodes.rationale: An officially supported demo channel running a chat UI on localhost:8787 with nothing to authenticate and no external service. Install `fakechat@claude-plugins-official`, restart with `--channels`, type in the browser and the message arrives in the session. The recommended way to learn the plugin flow before wiring a real platform.

nodes.label: Two named plugin-install failure modes
nodes.rationale: `Marketplace "claude-plugins-official" not found` means add the marketplace and retry. 'Plugin not found in the marketplace' means check the name — Claude Code already refreshes a stale catalog and retries before reporting it, so with marketplace auto-update off you refresh manually first. An install summary saying `Run /reload-plugins to activate.` must be obeyed unless a restart follows anyway.

nodes.label: --channels is the per-session opt-in
nodes.rationale: No channel runs until a user opts it in for the session with `--channels`, which accepts several space-separated plugins. The startup screen shows a channels notice naming what injects into the session, with a warning line below it if a plugin is not installed or not on the approved allowlist.

nodes.label: Being in .mcp.json is not enough to push messages
nodes.rationale: A server must ALSO be named in `--channels`. Registration as an ordinary MCP server grants query access, never push access — the two are separate gates.

nodes.label: How a channel event reaches the terminal and the model
nodes.rationale: The terminal shows an inbound channel line such as `← fakechat · web: <message>`, while the model receives a `<channel source="plugin:fakechat:fakechat">` event using the plugin's SCOPED server name. Claude then calls the channel's `reply` tool, whose first use triggers a permission prompt.

nodes.label: Every approved channel plugin keeps a sender allowlist
nodes.rationale: Only IDs you have added can push messages; everyone else is SILENTLY DROPPED. Telegram and Discord bootstrap the list by pairing — message the bot, it returns a code, you approve the code in session, and your sender ID is added. iMessage bootstraps by self-chat instead.

nodes.label: The allowlist also gates permission relay — an authority decision
nodes.rationale: If the channel declares permission relay, ANYONE who can reply through it can approve or deny tool use in your session. So allowlisting a sender is not only granting them the ability to ask — it is granting them authority over your permission prompts.

nodes.label: A permission prompt pauses the session until answered
nodes.rationale: If Claude hits a prompt while you are away, the session pauses. Channel servers declaring the permission relay capability can forward prompts for remote approval. `--dangerously-skip-permissions` bypasses most prompts for unattended use, but explicit ask rules, org-set `ask` connector tools, and MCP tools marked `requiresUserInteraction` still prompt.

nodes.label: Non-interactive mode disables tools that need terminal input
nodes.rationale: Running channels with `-p` disables tools requiring terminal input — multiple-choice questions and plan-mode approval — so the session never stalls waiting for input that cannot arrive.

nodes.label: channelsEnabled — the master switch
nodes.rationale: Must be `true` for any channel to deliver messages, and it blocks all channels INCLUDING the development flag when off. Default depends on authentication: claude.ai Team and Enterprise block channels until an Owner enables them; Console with API-key auth permits them unless the org deploys managed settings. Pro and Max users without an organization skip these checks entirely.

nodes.label: With channels disabled the MCP server still works — messages just never arrive
nodes.rationale: If `channelsEnabled` is disabled or unset, the MCP server still connects and its tools work, but channel messages do not arrive. A startup warning tells the user to have an admin enable the setting — the only signal distinguishing 'disabled' from 'nobody messaged me'.

nodes.label: allowedChannelPlugins REPLACES the Anthropic allowlist
nodes.rationale: Each entry names a plugin and its marketplace. When set it replaces the Anthropic list ENTIRELY — only listed plugins register. Leave it unset to fall back to the default. It requires `channelsEnabled: true`, and a user passing an unlisted plugin gets a normal startup with an explanatory notice rather than an error.

nodes.label: An empty allowedChannelPlugins does NOT block everything
nodes.rationale: An empty array blocks every allowlisted plugin, but `--dangerously-load-development-channels` can still bypass that block for local testing. To block channels entirely INCLUDING the development flag, leave `channelsEnabled` unset instead. The intuitive lockdown is the weaker one.

nodes.label: --dangerously-load-development-channels for a channel you are building
nodes.rationale: During the preview `--channels` only accepts plugins from the Anthropic-maintained allowlist or the organization's own. To test a channel you are building, use the development flag — which `channelsEnabled: false` still blocks, but an empty `allowedChannelPlugins` does not.

nodes.label: How channels compare to the other outside-the-terminal features
nodes.rationale: Claude Code on the web runs tasks in a fresh cloud sandbox; Claude in Slack spawns a web session from an @Claude mention; a standard MCP server is QUERIED during a task with nothing pushed; Remote Control drives your local session from claude.ai or mobile. Channels fill the gap by pushing events from non-Claude sources into an already-running LOCAL session.

nodes.label: The two shapes channels are for
nodes.rationale: A chat bridge — ask from your phone via Telegram/Discord/iMessage and the answer returns in the same chat while the work runs on your machine against your real files. And a webhook receiver — a webhook from CI, an error tracker or a deploy pipeline arrives where Claude already has your files open and remembers what you were debugging.

nodes.label: Build your own channel
nodes.rationale: The Channels reference covers building a channel for systems without a plugin yet, including the permission-relay capability and the webhook-receiver example. Custom channels are tested with the development flag during the preview.

nodes.label: Every pre-built channel plugin requires Bun
nodes.rationale: The shipped channel plugins are Bun scripts, so `bun --version` must work before any of them will start. This is a hard prerequisite separate from Claude Code's own install.

nodes.label: Install channel plugins at USER scope
nodes.rationale: Each setup step says to choose the user scope option so the plugin is available across all your projects — a channel is a machine-level integration, not a per-repo one.

nodes.label: Telegram bots come from BotFather
nodes.rationale: Send `/newbot` to BotFather, give a display name and a unique username ending in `bot`, and copy the returned token. The token is the entire credential — there is no separate app registration.

nodes.label: Discord needs Message Content Intent enabled explicitly
nodes.rationale: Under Privileged Gateway Intents in the bot's settings. Without it the bot connects but cannot read message text, which looks like an unresponsive channel rather than a permission error.

nodes.label: The Discord invite needs six specific permissions
nodes.rationale: Via OAuth2 > URL Generator with the `bot` scope: View Channels, Send Messages, Send Messages in Threads, Read Message History, Attach Files, and Add Reactions.

nodes.label: iMessage needs Full Disk Access for the app that launched Bun
nodes.rationale: macOS protects `~/Library/Messages/chat.db`; the prompt names whichever app launched Bun — Terminal, iTerm, or your IDE — not Claude Code. Without it the server exits immediately with `authorization denied`, so the failure is at startup rather than at first message.

nodes.label: The bot can only reply while the channel is active
nodes.rationale: Repeated in both the Telegram and Discord pairing steps: if the bot does not respond to your pairing message, Claude Code is not running with `--channels`. A silent bot is the expected symptom of a channel that was never started.

nodes.label: Permission relay is a declared channel capability
nodes.rationale: Only channel servers that DECLARE the relay capability can forward permission prompts for remote approval. It is opt-in per channel, not a property of channels in general — and it is what makes the sender allowlist an authority decision.

nodes.label: The startup notice is the diagnostic surface
nodes.rationale: It states which servers inject into this session, and adds a warning line naming the problem when a plugin is not installed or not on the approved allowlist. A channel that will never deliver says so at startup rather than at first message.

nodes.label: Orchestrate subagents at scale with dynamic workflows
nodes.rationale: A dynamic workflow is a JavaScript script that orchestrates subagents at scale. Claude writes the script for the task you describe and a runtime executes it in the background while your session stays responsive. Requires v2.1.154 or later; on Pro it must be turned on from the Dynamic workflows row in `/config`.

nodes.label: Reach for a workflow when one conversation cannot coordinate the agents
nodes.rationale: The stated triggers: a task needing more agents than one conversation can coordinate, or wanting the orchestration codified as a readable, rerunnable script. Examples — a codebase-wide bug sweep, a 500-file migration, research needing sources cross-checked, and a hard plan worth drafting from several independent angles before committing.

nodes.label: Subagents / skills / agent teams / workflows differ by WHO HOLDS THE PLAN
nodes.rationale: With subagents, skills and agent teams Claude is the orchestrator deciding turn by turn, and every result lands in a context window. A workflow script holds the loop, the branching and the intermediate results itself, so Claude's context holds only the final answer. Scale: a few tasks per turn vs dozens to hundreds of agents per run.

nodes.label: Moving the plan into code enables repeatable QUALITY patterns
nodes.rationale: Not just more agents: a workflow can have independent agents ADVERSARIALLY REVIEW each other's findings before they are reported, or draft a plan from several angles and weigh them against each other — a more trustworthy result than a single pass.

nodes.label: /deep-research — the one bundled workflow
nodes.rationale: Fans out web searches across several angles, fetches and cross-checks the sources, votes on each claim, and returns a cited report with claims that failed cross-checking filtered out. Requires the WebSearch tool. It runs ONLY when you invoke it — before v2.1.218 Claude could start it on its own.

nodes.label: An unverifiable claim is reported as unverified, not refuted (v2.1.196)
nodes.rationale: When verifier agents cannot check a claim — after a rate limit or API error — the report lists it as UNVERIFIED rather than counting it as refuted. A distinction between 'checked and false' and 'never asked', made in the product itself.

nodes.label: /workflows progress view and its key bindings
nodes.rationale: Lists running and completed runs with each phase's agent count, token total and elapsed time. Keys: arrows select; Enter/-> drills into a phase then an agent to read its prompt, recent tool calls and result; Esc/<- backs out (in v2.1.203-v2.1.205 `<-` did not, use Esc); j/k scroll; f filters by status; p pauses/resumes; x stops an agent or the run; s saves the script as a command.

nodes.label: The task panel shows a one-line progress summary
nodes.rationale: Below the input box a one-line progress summary appears while a run is going; the down arrow focuses it and Enter expands. This is also where the Large workflow warning surfaces.

nodes.label: The ultracode keyword opts one prompt into a workflow
nodes.rationale: Including `ultracode` in a prompt runs that single task as a workflow WITHOUT changing session effort. Asking in your own words ('use a workflow', 'run a workflow') is treated as the same opt-in. Before v2.1.160 the literal trigger was `workflow`; natural-language requests work in both.

nodes.label: The keyword chooses structure, not permissions
nodes.rationale: A workflow started by keyword runs inside the session's EXISTING permission mode, and its agents' tool calls receive the same permission checks and sandboxing as any other tool call. Opting into a workflow is not opting into looser permissions.

nodes.label: The keyword only triggers from human-typed input
nodes.rationale: It is an opt-in only at the interactive prompt, an IDE panel, a Remote Control client, or an Agent SDK app stamping origin `{kind: "human"}`. It does NOT start a workflow from `-p`, an unstamped SDK prompt, a scheduled task, or a webhook payload / PR comment relayed into the conversation. Before v2.1.210 all of those routes did trigger it.

nodes.label: Dismissing or disabling the keyword
nodes.rationale: Option+W on macOS or Alt+W elsewhere dismisses the highlight for that prompt, as does backspace with the cursor right after the highlighted keyword. Turn off 'Ultracode keyword trigger' in `/config` to stop it triggering at all.

nodes.label: ultracode as a session setting — Claude decides per task
nodes.rationale: `/effort ultracode` combines `xhigh` reasoning with automatic workflow orchestration; Claude then plans a workflow for each substantive task without being asked, and a single request can become SEVERAL workflows in a row — understand, change, verify. Session-only, resets on a new session; requires v2.1.203 and a model supporting `xhigh`.

nodes.label: The per-run approval prompt
nodes.rationale: Shows the planned phases with Yes / Yes-and-don't-ask-again-for-this-workflow-in-this-project / View raw script / No. Ctrl+G opens the script in your editor and Tab lets you adjust the prompt first. The Desktop app shows an approval card with the name, phase list, a token-usage caution, and Once / Always / Deny.

nodes.label: When you are prompted depends on permission mode
nodes.rationale: Default and accept-edits prompt on every run unless you chose don't-ask-again for that workflow in that project. Auto mode prompts on first launch only, records consent in user settings, and skips entirely when ultracode is on. Bypass permissions, `claude -p` and the Agent SDK never prompt — the run starts immediately.

nodes.label: Workflow subagents ALWAYS run in acceptEdits mode
nodes.rationale: Your permission mode controls only the LAUNCH prompt. The subagents a workflow spawns always run in `acceptEdits` and inherit your tool allowlist regardless of the session's mode — file edits are auto-approved. Shell commands, web fetches and MCP tools outside the allowlist can still prompt mid-run, so add what the agents need before a long run.

nodes.label: Save a run's script as a command with `s`
nodes.rationale: From `/workflows`, select the run and press `s`. Tab toggles between `.claude/workflows/` in the project (shared with everyone who clones the repo) and `~/.claude/workflows/` (every project, visible only to you; honors `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`). The workflow then runs as `/<name>` and appears in `/` autocomplete alongside bundled ones.

nodes.label: The save path refuses to write through a symlink (v2.1.216)
nodes.rationale: Project location: refuses if `.claude`, `.claude/workflows`, or the target file is a symlink. Personal location: refuses only if the TARGET FILE itself is a symlink, so a dotfiles-managed `~/.claude` directory still works. Before v2.1.216 Claude Code followed the link, which could place the file outside the chosen location.

nodes.label: Monorepo workflow resolution — closest wins
nodes.rationale: As of v2.1.178, saving to the project location writes to the closest existing `.claude/workflows/` between the working directory and the repo root, or the repo root if none exists. Workflows load from EVERY such directory along that path, and when two define the same name the one closest to the working directory runs. A project workflow beats a personal one of the same name.

nodes.label: Distribute a workflow in a plugin
nodes.rationale: Place the script in a `workflows/` directory at the plugin root, or point elsewhere with the `workflows` manifest field. Plugin workflows are NAMESPACED: a plugin `acme-tools` with `meta.name` `release-audit` runs as `/acme-tools:release-audit`.

nodes.label: args passes structured input to a saved workflow
nodes.rationale: The script reads a global named `args` — a research question, a list of target paths, a configuration object — supplied at invocation instead of editing the script. Claude passes it as STRUCTURED DATA, so the script can call array and object methods directly without parsing. If omitted, the global is `undefined`.

nodes.label: What a saved script looks like
nodes.rationale: A `meta` block (name, description) followed by plain JavaScript with top-level `await`. `agent()` spawns one subagent; `pipeline()` runs one per item in a list. An `agent()` call resolves to `null` if stopped mid-run or on an unrecoverable API error, and `pipeline()` keeps that `null` — which is why examples end with `.filter(Boolean)`.

nodes.label: The runtime is isolated from the conversation
nodes.rationale: The script executes in an isolated environment separate from your conversation, with intermediate results staying in script variables instead of landing in Claude's context. Every run writes its script to a file under the session's directory in `~/.claude/projects/`, and Claude receives that path — so you can read it, diff it against a previous run, or edit it and relaunch.

nodes.label: The four runtime constraints
nodes.rationale: No mid-run user input — only agent permission prompts can pause a run, so sign-off between stages means running each stage as its own workflow. No direct filesystem or shell access from the script; agents do that and the script coordinates. Up to 16 concurrent agents, fewer on limited CPU. 1,000 agents total per run as a runaway-loop backstop.

nodes.label: Resume replays in START ORDER, which is what makes stopping expensive
nodes.rationale: An agent still running when you stopped is not saved and starts over. Cached results stop at the FIRST agent that did not finish, and every agent that started after it re-runs even if it completed. Stop while B of A,B,C,D is going and C and D both re-run. So a fan-out across many small agents preserves more progress than one long agent.

nodes.label: Resume works only within the same session
nodes.rationale: Resume a paused run from `/workflows` with `p`, or ask Claude to relaunch with the same script. If you exit Claude Code while a workflow is running, the next session starts the workflow FRESH — nothing carries across.

nodes.label: Cost — run on a small slice before committing
nodes.rationale: A single run can use meaningfully more tokens than the same task in conversation, and counts toward plan usage and rate limits. The documented way to gauge spend is to run it on a SMALL SLICE first — one directory instead of the whole repo, a narrow question instead of a broad one — watching per-agent token usage in `/workflows` and stopping there if needed.

nodes.label: The Large workflow warning is advisory only
nodes.rationale: When a run schedules more than 25 agents or projects over 1.5 million tokens, the task-panel progress line shows a `Large workflow` warning pointing at `/workflows`. It does NOT pause or limit the run. A chosen size guideline's agent count replaces the 25 threshold, and ultracode sessions do not show it at all. Requires v2.1.203.

nodes.label: workflowSizeGuideline is advice to Claude, not a cap
nodes.rationale: `unrestricted` (no guideline), `small` (<5 agents), `medium` (<15), `large` (<50). Sent to Claude as ADVICE, so a prompt calling for a different scale still overrides it. Default is `medium` from v2.1.219; earlier versions default to `unrestricted`. A settings-file value takes precedence over `/config` and hides the `/config` row. Runtime caps still apply regardless.

nodes.label: Every workflow agent uses the session model unless overridden
nodes.rationale: Unless the script routes a stage to a different model or `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL` is set — which overrides BOTH. To control model cost, check `/model` before a large run, and ask Claude to use a smaller model for stages that do not need the strongest one.

nodes.label: Turning workflows off, per user and per organization
nodes.rationale: Per user: the `/config` toggle, `"disableWorkflows": true` in `~/.claude/settings.json`, or `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_WORKFLOWS=1` read at startup. Org-wide: `disableWorkflows` in managed settings or the admin-settings toggle. When disabled, bundled workflow commands vanish, the `ultracode` keyword stops triggering, and `ultracode` is removed from the `/effort` menu.

nodes.label: Six example workflow shapes
nodes.rationale: Audit many files then adversarially verify each finding; keep fixing until a check passes or two rounds make no progress; migrate files in parallel each in its own isolated copy; review every changed file then merge into one ranked summary; research a topic across many sources in parallel then compare; and find issues in rounds until two rounds turn up nothing new.

nodes.label: Dynamic workflows require v2.1.154 or later
nodes.rationale: Available on all paid plans, with Anthropic API access, and on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform and Microsoft Foundry. On Pro they must be turned on from the Dynamic workflows row in `/config` — so a Pro session's absence of workflows is a setting, not a plan limit.

nodes.label: Shape: audit many files, then adversarially verify each finding
nodes.rationale: Fan out one agent per file, then collect and verify. The documented prompt asks explicitly to 'adversarially verify each finding before reporting it' — verification is part of the request, not an afterthought.

nodes.label: Shape: keep fixing until a check passes, or two rounds make no progress
nodes.rationale: Run a checker, fix what failed, repeat. The stop rule is doubled: pass OR two consecutive rounds without progress — a bound that prevents a non-converging loop from running to the agent cap.

nodes.label: Shape: migrate many files in parallel, each in an isolated copy
nodes.rationale: Discover the files, transform each one in its OWN isolated copy so edits do not conflict, and verify each result. Isolation is what makes per-file parallelism safe when the agents all write.

nodes.label: Shape: review every changed file, then merge into one ranked summary
nodes.rationale: A reviewer per file, then a single agent that ranks and DEDUPLICATES the per-file findings. The second stage exists because per-file reviewers cannot see each other's findings.

nodes.label: Shape: research across many sources, then compare
nodes.rationale: Fan out readers across changelogs, issues and docs in parallel, then synthesize. `/deep-research` is the bundled version; a narrower one can be described directly.

nodes.label: Shape: search in rounds until the list stops growing
nodes.rationale: Keep searching and stop once two rounds in a row find nothing new — the documented pattern for unknown-size discovery, where a fixed count would miss the tail.

nodes.label: Running the bundled workflow end to end
nodes.rationale: Invoke `/deep-research <question>`; approve when Claude Code asks (the exact prompt depends on permission mode); watch via `/workflows` or the task panel; then read the report, which lands in the session with sources cited and unsupported claims filtered out.

nodes.label: Drilling into a phase reveals each agent's prompt and tool calls
nodes.rationale: The progress view is not just a counter: Enter drills into a phase and then into an individual agent to read its PROMPT, its recent tool calls, and its result — which is how you audit what a run actually did.

nodes.label: Individual agents can be stopped or restarted mid-run
nodes.rationale: `x` stops the selected agent, or the whole workflow when focus is on the run; `r` restarts the selected RUNNING agent. So a single wedged agent does not require killing the run.

nodes.label: Ctrl+G opens the planned script in your editor before approval
nodes.rationale: Alongside 'View raw script' in the approval prompt, Ctrl+G opens it in your editor and Tab lets you adjust the prompt before the run starts — the script is reviewable BEFORE any agent spawns.

nodes.label: Two save locations, and which one wins
nodes.rationale: `.claude/workflows/` in the project is shared with everyone who clones the repo; `~/.claude/workflows/` is available in every project and visible only to you, honoring `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`. If a project workflow and a personal workflow share a name, the PROJECT one runs.

nodes.label: The save dialog shows the resolved personal path (v2.1.208)
nodes.rationale: Before v2.1.208 it displayed `~/.claude/workflows/` even when `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` was set — the file was still saved under the configured directory, so the displayed path was wrong while the behavior was right.

nodes.label: Resume a paused run with `p`, or ask Claude to relaunch
nodes.rationale: From `/workflows`, select the run and press `p`; alternatively ask Claude to relaunch the workflow with the same script. Both are session-bound.

nodes.label: Three ways to set the size guideline, and their precedence
nodes.rationale: The Dynamic workflow size row in `/config`, `/config workflowSizeGuideline=small`, or (v2.1.219+) the `workflowSizeGuideline` key in any settings file. A settings-file value takes PRECEDENCE over `/config` and hides the `/config` row entirely. Changes take effect on the next prompt.

nodes.label: The script coordinates; only agents touch the filesystem
nodes.rationale: The workflow itself has no direct filesystem or shell access. Agents read, write and run commands; the script holds the loop, the branching and the results. This is why a workflow cannot be used to bypass a tool restriction.
